concepts.title: Lambda Expressions & Functional Interfaces
concepts.description: A lambda expression is a compact block of behavior with no name and no type of its own -- it only becomes meaningful once matched against a functional interface, an interface with exactly one abstract method, and that matching (plus a strict rule about which local variables a lambda may read) is what makes lambdas both powerful and occasionally surprising.
learningObjectives: Define what a functional interface is and explain why it must have exactly one abstract method.
Write a lambda expression and explain how both its parameter types and its target interface are inferred from context.
Name and use at least four of the standard java.util.function interfaces: Function, Predicate, Consumer, and Supplier.
Use each of the four kinds of method references and explain when each one applies.
Explain why a lambda can read but not reassign a captured local variable, and connect this to the 'effectively final' rule.
Contrast a lambda's this with an anonymous inner class's this.

sections.heading: Functional Interfaces: An Interface With Exactly One Job
Lambda Syntax and Target Typing
sections.body:
A lambda expression has the shape `(parameters) -> body`, where the body is either a single expression (its value becomes the return value) or a `{ }`-braced block of statements (which needs explicit `return` if it produces a value). Parameter types are almost always omitted and inferred; parentheses around a single parameter can be dropped too.

```java
(String name) -> "Hello, " + name             // explicit parameter type
name -> "Hello, " + name                       // type inferred, parens optional for one param
(a, b) -> a + b                                // multiple params, types inferred
(a, b) -> { int sum = a + b; return sum; }     // block body needs an explicit return
```

Here's the detail that trips people up initially: a lambda expression, by itself, **has no type**. Its type is determined entirely by the context it's used in -- what Java calls **target typing**. The same lambda literal can implement completely different functional interfaces depending purely on where it's assigned or passed.

```java
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("running");            // target type: Runnable
Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("running"));  // same-shaped lambda, target type inferred from Thread's constructor parameter
```

Both lambdas above look identical -- `() -> System.out.println("running")` -- but the first is being matched against `Runnable`'s `run()` method because that's the declared type of `r`, and the second is being matched against whatever functional interface `Thread`'s constructor parameter expects (also `Runnable`, as it happens, but the point stands: it's the *context*, not the lambda text itself, doing the matching).

sections.heading: The Standard Toolkit: java.util.function
sections.body:
Rather than writing a new one-method interface every time you need to pass around a small piece of behavior, `java.util.function` provides a set of general-purpose functional interfaces covering the overwhelmingly common shapes:

- `Function<T, R>` -- one method, `R apply(T t)` -- takes a `T`, produces an `R`.
- `Predicate<T>` -- one method, `boolean test(T t)` -- takes a `T`, returns true/false.
- `Consumer<T>` -- one method, `void accept(T t)` -- takes a `T`, returns nothing (pure side effect).
- `Supplier<T>` -- one method, `T get()` -- takes nothing, produces a `T`.

```java
Function<String, Integer> length = s -> s.length();
Predicate<String> isBlank = s -> s.trim().isEmpty();
Consumer<String> print = s -> System.out.println(s);
Supplier<String> greeting = () -> "Hello!";

System.out.println(length.apply("hi"));   // 2
System.out.println(isBlank.test("   "));  // true
print.accept(greeting.get());              // prints "Hello!"
```

Several of these interfaces also carry useful `default` methods for composing them without writing a brand-new lambda from scratch: `Predicate.and`, `.or`, and `.negate()` combine predicates logically; `Function.andThen` and `.compose` chain two functions together, differing in which one runs first (covered directly in this concept's exercises). Learning to recognize these four shapes -- 'takes X, returns Y', 'takes X, returns boolean', 'takes X, returns nothing', 'takes nothing, returns Y' -- covers a large fraction of the lambdas you'll actually write.

sections.heading: Method References: Four Flavors of 'Just Call This Existing Method'
Variable Capture: Effectively Final, and this Inside a Lambda

examples.title: Target Typing: The Same Lambda Literal, Two Different Interfaces
examples.explanation: The exact same lambda text, (a, b) -> a + b, is written twice, and it means something structurally different each time purely because of the variable it's assigned to. The first assignment targets Calculator, a custom functional interface whose single abstract method is compute(int, int) -- so the lambda is understood as an implementation of compute. The second assignment targets BinaryOperator<Integer> (a standard functional interface with a single method apply(T, T)) -- the SAME lambda text is now understood as an implementation of apply, working with boxed Integer values instead of raw ints. This is target typing in action: a lambda expression has no fixed type of its own; the compiler determines what it implements entirely from the declared type it's being assigned to or passed as.

examples.title: The Four Kinds of Method References, Side by Side
examples.explanation: Each method reference is standing in for a lambda that does nothing but forward to one existing method. Integer::parseInt is a static method, so parse.apply("42") is exactly like calling Integer.parseInt("42") directly. log::add refers to the add method on one SPECIFIC, already-existing List instance (log) -- calling append.accept(...) always adds to that same list. String::toUpperCase is different: there's no specific String object named anywhere -- instead, whatever single argument upper.apply(...) is called with becomes the object toUpperCase() is invoked ON, which is why it works as a Function<String, String> taking one parameter. ArrayList::new is a constructor reference -- calling newList.get() is equivalent to writing new ArrayList<>() inline, useful anywhere a Supplier of a fresh instance is needed without writing out a full lambda.

examples.title: Effectively Final Capture: What Compiles, and the Mutable-Counter Workaround
examples.explanation: threshold is captured freely because it's assigned exactly once and never reassigned anywhere -- it's effectively final, satisfying the rule even without the explicit final keyword. The commented-out block shows what does NOT compile: total += n inside the lambda would reassign total, and Java requires captured local variables to never be reassigned anywhere in their enclosing scope, so this fails at compile time with an error about total not being final or effectively final. The AtomicInteger version works around this correctly: runningTotal itself, as a variable, is only ever assigned once (effectively final), so it's a legal capture -- what changes across each call is the OBJECT it points to internally (via addAndGet, a genuine mutation of that object's own state), not the reference stored in the local variable runningTotal itself. This is the standard idiom whenever a lambda genuinely needs to accumulate mutable state across multiple invocations.

misconceptions.description: A lambda expression has a fixed type of its own -- for example, x -> x * 2 'is a Function'.
misconceptions.clarification: A lambda expression has no type in isolation; it only becomes meaningful, and only acquires a type, once matched against a target functional interface determined by the context it's used in -- an assignment's declared type, a method parameter's declared type, or an explicit cast. The exact same lambda literal, x -> x * 2, could implement Function<Integer, Integer>, UnaryOperator<Integer>, or any custom functional interface with a single int-to-int-shaped abstract method, depending purely on where it's written. There is no such thing as 'the type of a lambda' without first asking 'assigned to what?'

misconceptions.description: A lambda captures local variables the way closures do in languages like JavaScript or Python -- it keeps a live, mutable connection to the variable, seeing any later reassignment.
misconceptions.clarification: Java lambdas may only capture local variables that are effectively final -- never reassigned anywhere in their enclosing scope after their initial assignment. The compiler rejects, at compile time, any attempt to capture a variable that's reassigned, precisely to avoid the exact live-mutable-capture ambiguity those other languages embrace. When a lambda genuinely needs access to shared, changing state, the idiomatic Java workaround is to capture a reference to a mutable container -- a one-element array, or an AtomicInteger / AtomicReference -- whose reference itself stays effectively final even as the container's own contents are mutated through method calls.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to count how many times run() is called, but it fails to compile. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: Look at what the lambda body does to count -- is count assigned to more than once anywhere in this method?
Local variables captured by a lambda must be effectively final -- never reassigned after their initial assignment, anywhere in their enclosing scope.
Replace the plain int with a mutable container whose reference itself never changes, such as an AtomicInteger, and call a method on it to both increment and read the value.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code fails to compile because count++ inside the lambda reassigns count, which disqualifies it from being effectively final -- and Java requires every local variable captured by a lambda to be effectively final, precisely because the lambda might be invoked later, or from elsewhere, with no well-defined single answer for 'which value did it capture' if the variable were allowed to keep changing underneath it. The fix replaces the plain int with an AtomicInteger: the LOCAL VARIABLE count is now only ever assigned once (to the new AtomicInteger(0) object), which satisfies the effectively-final rule, while incrementAndGet() mutates the internal state of that one object rather than reassigning the variable itself. Each call to r.run() correctly increments and prints an incrementing count: 1, then 2.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? Pay close attention to the difference between andThen and compose.
hints: f.andThen(g) means 'run f first, then run g on f's result' -- for combinedA, that means doubleIt runs first.
f.compose(g) means 'run g first, then run f on g's result' -- the order is the REVERSE of andThen. For combinedB, that means addTen runs first.
Compute combinedA.apply(5) step by step: doubleIt(5) first, then addTen on that result. Then do the same for combinedB, but with the two steps swapped.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 20, then 30. combinedA (andThen) computes doubleIt(5)=10, then addTen(10)=20. combinedB (compose) computes addTen(5)=15, then doubleIt(15)=30.
exercises.solutionExplanation: doubleIt.andThen(addTen) means: apply doubleIt FIRST, then feed its result into addTen. Calling combinedA.apply(5) therefore computes doubleIt(5) = 10 first, then addTen(10) = 20 -- printing 20. doubleIt.compose(addTen) means the reverse: apply addTen FIRST, then feed its result into doubleIt. Calling combinedB.apply(5) therefore computes addTen(5) = 15 first, then doubleIt(15) = 30 -- printing 30. andThen and compose both chain the exact same two functions together, but they differ in which one is considered to run first -- andThen reads left-to-right in the order you called the methods, while compose reads right-to-left, running its argument first and the original function second.

assessments.prompt: Why must a functional interface have exactly one abstract method, no more and no fewer?
options: It's an arbitrary restriction the JDK team chose to keep interfaces simple; it has no real technical necessity.

A lambda's body is just an expression or block of statements with no method name attached -- the compiler needs exactly one unambiguous abstract method signature on the target interface to know what that body is implementing.
Having more than one abstract method would make the interface too slow to call at run time.
Java requires this only for interfaces explicitly annotated @FunctionalInterface; unannotated interfaces can have any number of abstract methods and still be used with a lambda.
assessments.explanation: Option B identifies the real, structural reason: a lambda expression carries no method name at all, so matching it against an interface requires exactly one abstract method slot for the compiler to unambiguously bind the lambda's parameters and body to. With two or more abstract methods, there would be no way to know which one the lambda's body is meant to implement. Option A is wrong -- this is a genuine technical necessity, not an arbitrary style choice. Option C is wrong -- this has nothing to do with runtime performance. Option D is wrong and worth flagging directly: @FunctionalInterface is optional documentation-plus-compiler-check, not the mechanism that makes the one-abstract-method rule apply -- any interface with exactly one abstract method can be used as a lambda's target type whether or not it carries that annotation, and adding the annotation to an interface with two or more abstract methods is itself a compile error.

assessments.prompt: Explain to someone who understands methods and interfaces, but has never used lambdas, what a lambda expression actually is, how target typing determines what it implements, and why it can only read (not reassign) certain local variables from its surroundings.
assessments.modelAnswer: A lambda expression is a compact, inline way of writing the single method body of an implementation of a functional interface -- an interface that declares exactly one abstract method -- without writing out a full named class or an anonymous class for it. Something like name -> "Hello, " + name is, by itself, just a description of 'take one parameter, produce this expression's value' -- it has no fixed type or identity on its own. What gives it meaning is target typing: wherever that lambda is actually written -- assigned to a variable of some functional interface type, passed as an argument to a parameter of some functional interface type, or explicitly cast -- the compiler looks at that specific context to determine which functional interface's single abstract method the lambda is meant to implement, and checks that the lambda's parameter count and body are compatible with that method's signature. The exact same lambda text can implement completely different functional interfaces in two different places, purely because of what it's assigned to in each case; there's no such thing as 'the type of this lambda' independent of that context. As for variable capture: a lambda body is allowed to read local variables and parameters from its enclosing scope, but only ones that are 'effectively final' -- assigned exactly once and never reassigned anywhere afterward in that scope, even if the final keyword isn't explicitly written. This exists because a lambda can genuinely be invoked later than, and separately from, the method call that created it -- stored in a field, handed to another thread, called back after the original method has already returned -- and if the captured variable were allowed to keep changing, there would be no single well-defined answer for which value the lambda should actually see. Rather than trying to define some complicated live-capture semantics, Java simply disallows capturing anything that changes, and pushes anyone who genuinely needs shared, mutable state accessed from inside a lambda toward capturing a reference to a mutable container object instead -- the reference stays effectively final even while the object's own internal state changes through its own methods.

assessments.prompt: Function<String, Integer> len = String::length; What does this method reference actually mean, given that no specific String object appears anywhere in the expression?
options: It calls length() on a fixed, hidden String object that the JVM creates internally every time len.apply(...) is called.

It's an instance method reference on an arbitrary object of a given type: whatever single argument is passed to len.apply(...) becomes the object that length() is actually called on, exactly equivalent to writing s -> s.length().
This fails to compile, because an instance method can never be referenced without explicitly specifying a receiver object.
It treats length as if it were a static method of String, calling it with no receiver object at all.
assessments.explanation: This is the third of the four method-reference forms: when the referenced method is an instance method and no specific object is named, the lambda's own incoming parameter becomes the receiver the method is called on. Function<String, Integer> takes one String argument and returns an Integer, and s.length() matches that shape exactly, with s supplied at call time as len.apply(s). Option A invents a hidden object that doesn't exist. Option C is wrong -- this exact form (an instance method reference on an arbitrary object of a type) is one of the four standard, fully legal method reference forms. Option D is wrong because length() is a genuine instance method on String, not a static one; the method reference works precisely because the argument becomes the receiver, not because the method is static.

assessments.prompt: List<Runnable> tasks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { int current = i; tasks.add(() -> System.out.println(current)); } Why does this compile, when capturing the loop variable i directly -- tasks.add(() -> System.out.println(i)); -- would not?
options: current and i are actually the same variable under the hood, so there's no real difference -- both versions would compile identically.

current is a brand-new local variable, freshly declared and assigned exactly once within each loop iteration, so it's effectively final for that iteration's lambda; i, by contrast, is reassigned by the loop's own update step (i++) on every iteration, which disqualifies it from being effectively final.
Lambdas can only capture variables declared with the exact keyword final, and current happens to satisfy that requirement while i does not.
This fails to compile as written too, because ArrayList cannot hold a list of lambdas.
assessments.explanation: Each pass through the loop body declares a fresh current and assigns it exactly once, so from the lambda's point of view inside that one iteration, current is never reassigned anywhere in its scope -- effectively final. i, however, is a single variable shared across every iteration, and the loop's update clause reassigns it on every pass, which makes it fail the effectively-final test regardless of which iteration's lambda tries to capture it. Option A is wrong -- current and i are genuinely different variables, with different values captured across iterations, which is exactly why the copy-into-current pattern is a standard idiom. Option C overstates the rule -- effectively final variables don't need the explicit final keyword at all, only the never-reassigned property. Option D is a fabricated, unrelated claim; ArrayList holds references of any type, lambdas included.

assessments.prompt: class Handler { private String label = "handler"; Runnable makeLambdaRunnable() { return () -> System.out.println(this.label); } Runnable makeAnonymousRunnable() { return new Runnable() { public void run() { System.out.println(this.label); } }; } } What is true about each method?
options: Both compile fine and print "handler", because this always refers to the enclosing Handler instance inside both a lambda and an anonymous class.

makeLambdaRunnable() compiles fine -- a lambda introduces no instance or this of its own, so this.label correctly refers to the enclosing Handler's field; makeAnonymousRunnable() fails to compile, because the anonymous class genuinely creates its own object with its own this, which has no field named label, requiring Handler.this.label to reach the enclosing instance instead.
Both fail to compile, because this can never be referenced inside any implementation of a functional interface.
makeAnonymousRunnable() compiles fine and makeLambdaRunnable() fails, because lambdas are never allowed to reference this under any circumstance.
assessments.explanation: A lambda body behaves as if it were written directly inline in the enclosing code -- it introduces no new this at all, so this.label inside the lambda resolves to Handler's own label field exactly as it would anywhere else in makeLambdaRunnable. An anonymous class, by contrast, genuinely creates a distinct object of its own, with its own this -- and that anonymous Runnable object has no field named label, so this.label inside its run() method fails to compile (there being no such member to resolve to); reaching the enclosing Handler's label from inside the anonymous class requires the more verbose Handler.this.label. Option A ignores this real, structural difference. Option C is wrong -- this is used constantly and correctly inside lambdas, referring to the enclosing context. Option D reverses which one actually has the problem.

concepts.title: The Stream API: map, filter, reduce, and collect
concepts.description: A Stream describes a pipeline over a source of data -- lazy intermediate operations like map and filter build up that description without doing any actual work, and nothing runs at all until a terminal operation like collect or reduce finally pulls elements through the whole chain, exactly once.
learningObjectives: Describe the three-part shape of a stream pipeline: a source, a chain of intermediate operations, and a terminal operation.
Explain why intermediate operations are lazy and only actually execute once a terminal operation is invoked.
Use map, filter, sorted, and distinct to transform a stream, and explain the difference between stateless and stateful intermediate operations.
Use reduce with an identity value and a combining function to fold a stream's elements into a single result.
Use collect with common Collectors (toList, toMap, groupingBy, joining) to gather stream results into a concrete structure.
Explain why a stream can only be consumed once, and predict the exception that results from reusing one.

sections.heading: The Shape of a Stream Pipeline: Source, Intermediate, Terminal
sections.body:
A `Stream` is not a data structure that stores elements the way a `List` does -- it's a description of a computation over some source of data. Every stream pipeline has the same three-part shape: a **source** (a collection's `.stream()`, `Stream.of(...)`, `IntStream.range(...)`, and so on), zero or more **intermediate operations** chained onto it (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`), and exactly one **terminal operation** that actually produces a non-stream result and ends the pipeline (`collect`, `reduce`, `forEach`, `count`, `anyMatch`, `findFirst`).

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Amy", "Ben", "cara", "Dev", "amy");

List<String> result = names.stream()          // source
    .filter(n -> n.length() <= 3)              // intermediate
    .map(String::toUpperCase)                  // intermediate
    .distinct()                                // intermediate
    .sorted()                                  // intermediate
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toList());  // terminal
```

Intermediate operations always return another `Stream`, which is what allows them to be chained fluently one after another; a terminal operation returns something else entirely -- a `List`, an `int`, a `boolean`, an `Optional` -- and once it runs, the pipeline is finished.

sections.heading: Laziness: Nothing Runs Until the Terminal Operation Is Invoked
map, filter, and the Stateless vs Stateful Distinction
sections.body:
`filter(Predicate<T>)` keeps only the elements that satisfy a condition, discarding the rest; `map(Function<T, R>)` transforms every element into some new value, possibly of a completely different type, one-to-one. Both are **stateless**: deciding what to do with one element never requires knowing anything about any other element in the stream.

`sorted()` and `distinct()`, by contrast, are **stateful**: `sorted()` fundamentally cannot know an element's correct final position until it's seen every other element it needs to be compared against, and `distinct()` has to remember every element it's already emitted in order to recognize a later duplicate. This distinction matters in practice: stateful operations generally need to buffer more of the stream at once, behave differently (and sometimes worse) on very large or infinite streams, and interact with parallel streams in ways that stateless operations like `map` and `filter` simply don't have to worry about.

```java
List<Integer> result = java.util.stream.Stream.of(5, 3, 5, 1, 3, 2)
    .distinct()   // [5, 3, 1, 2] -- must remember what it's already seen
    .sorted()     // [1, 2, 3, 5] -- must see everything before it can order anything
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toList());
```

sections.heading: reduce: Folding Everything Into One Value
sections.body:
`reduce` combines a stream's elements pairwise into a single result. The two-argument form, `reduce(identity, BinaryOperator<T>)`, takes a starting value (the **identity** -- also the correct result for an empty stream) and a function describing how to combine two values into one, applying it repeatedly across the whole stream.

```java
int sum = java.util.stream.Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4)
    .reduce(0, (a, b) -> a + b);   // 0+1=1, 1+2=3, 3+3=6, 6+4=10
System.out.println(sum);           // 10
```

There's also a one-argument overload, `reduce(BinaryOperator<T>)`, which has no identity value to fall back on -- and since there's genuinely no sensible answer for an empty stream without one, this overload returns `Optional<T>` instead of `T` directly, forcing the caller to explicitly consider the empty case. Reach for `reduce` when you're genuinely folding elements down into one summary value of the *same* type as the elements (a sum, a maximum, a concatenation); when the goal is instead to build up a *different* kind of result -- a `List`, a `Map`, a grouped structure -- `collect` is almost always the better, more idiomatic tool, covered next.

sections.heading: collect and Collectors: Building an Actual Result Structure

examples.title: A Full Pipeline: filter, map, sorted, collect
examples.explanation: filter(w -> w.length() > 3) keeps only words longer than 3 characters, dropping "fig" (length 3); map(String::toUpperCase) then transforms each surviving word to uppercase, one element at a time; sorted() orders the resulting strings alphabetically; and collect(Collectors.toList()) is the terminal operation that finally triggers all of this and gathers the result into an actual List. Nothing in this pipeline actually executes until collect is reached -- filter, map, and sorted each just add a step to the pipeline's description, in the exact order written, and elements are pulled through that whole chain only once the terminal operation demands a result.

examples.title: Laziness Made Visible
examples.explanation: The first pipeline calls .map(...) but attaches no terminal operation at all -- it compiles fine, and running it produces no "mapping ..." output whatsoever, because an intermediate operation with nothing pulling elements through it never actually executes; the whole statement is a silent no-op. The second pipeline is structurally identical except for one addition: .count() at the end, a terminal operation. That single addition is what causes the pipeline to actually run, printing "mapping amy", "mapping ben", "mapping cara" as each element is pulled through map on its way to being counted, before finally printing "count = 3". The map() lambda's own code is completely unchanged between the two versions -- what differs is purely whether anything downstream ever asks the pipeline to actually produce a result.

examples.title: reduce for a Single Summary Value vs collect for a Structured Result
examples.explanation: reduce(0, Integer::sum) folds the stream of individual word lengths down into a single int -- 0 is the identity (also the correct answer for an empty stream), and Integer::sum combines two lengths at a time into a running total, ending at 19. This is the right tool here because the desired result -- one summary number -- is fundamentally a single value of the same general kind (a number) being accumulated across the stream. collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length)), by contrast, isn't folding anything down to one value -- it's building an entirely different KIND of structure, a Map from each distinct length to the list of words that have that length. groupingBy applies String::length to each word to compute its key, and automatically buckets each word into a list under that key -- exactly the kind of structured, multi-shaped result that reduce is a poor fit for and collect handles directly.

misconceptions.description: Calling .filter(...) or .map(...) on a stream processes all the elements immediately, the same way calling a method on a List would.
misconceptions.clarification: Intermediate operations like filter and map are lazy -- calling them only records a step in the pipeline's description; no element is actually processed at that moment. Nothing runs at all until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count, and so on) is invoked, at which point elements are pulled through the ENTIRE chain of intermediate operations, typically one at a time. A direct, observable consequence is that a chain of intermediate operations with no terminal operation attached at all compiles perfectly fine and does absolutely nothing at run time -- a silent no-op, not an error.

misconceptions.description: A stream variable can have a terminal operation called on it more than once, the same way you can call .size() on a List as many times as you want.
misconceptions.clarification: A Stream can be traversed exactly once. The moment a terminal operation runs, that stream is considered consumed (the specification calls this 'operated upon or closed'), and any further operation attempted on that same stream reference -- even a completely different terminal operation -- throws IllegalStateException at run time: 'stream has already been operated upon or closed'. To run the same or a different pipeline again, you need a fresh stream, typically by calling .stream() again on the original underlying collection or source, not by reusing the old stream reference.

exercises.prompt: This code is supposed to print how many words are longer than 3 letters, and then print the uppercase versions of those same words. Instead, it throws IllegalStateException at runtime. Find and fix the bug.
hints: longWords is a single Stream reference -- how many terminal operations does this code call on that same reference?
count() is itself a terminal operation, even though it doesn't look like it 'consumes' anything visually -- what happens to a stream once ANY terminal operation has run on it?
You need two SEPARATE streams for two separate pipelines -- build one from words.stream() for the count, and a fresh one from words.stream() again for the map-and-collect.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code builds one Stream, longWords, and then calls count() on it -- count() is a terminal operation, so once it runs, longWords is fully consumed, even though the code never explicitly reassigns or discards the variable. The very next line calls .map(...) on that same, already-consumed longWords reference, which throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. The fix builds a completely separate stream, starting fresh from words.stream(), for each independent pipeline -- one for the count, and another, freshly created one, for the filter-map-collect chain. Streams are a one-shot description of a computation, not a reusable data structure, so any time you need to run more than one pipeline over the same source, you create more than one stream from that source.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, in order? Pay attention to what distinct() and sorted() each do, and in which order they run.
hints: distinct() removes duplicates but does not change relative order among the elements it keeps.
sorted() puts elements into ascending order regardless of what order they arrived in.

Trace resultA: remove duplicates from {4,1,4,3,2,1,4} first (keeping first-seen order), THEN sort what's left. Then trace resultB with the two steps swapped -- does the FINAL result actually end up different?
exercises.expectedAnswer:
[1, 2, 3, 4]
[1, 2, 3, 4]
Both pipelines produce the same final list, even though distinct() and sorted() run in a different order in each -- distinct-then-sort and sort-then-distinct happen to agree here because sorting doesn't introduce or remove duplicates, and removing duplicates doesn't disturb sorted order once it's already established.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For resultA: distinct() first reduces {4,1,4,3,2,1,4} to {4,1,3,2} (keeping each value's first occurrence, dropping later repeats), and then sorted() orders that down to [1,2,3,4]. For resultB: sorted() first orders the original list to [1,1,2,3,4,4,4], and then distinct() removes the now-adjacent duplicates, also landing on [1,2,3,4]. Both pipelines print the identical final list. This isn't a coincidence specific to this data -- sorting a list never creates or removes duplicate VALUES (it only reorders them), and removing duplicates from an already-sorted list never disturbs the sortedness of what remains, so distinct-then-sort and sort-then-distinct are actually guaranteed to agree on the final set and order of elements in general, even though the two pipelines do meaningfully different amounts of work to get there (sorting a larger, not-yet-deduplicated list versus a smaller, already-deduplicated one).

options: filter() has already run and produced a filtered Stream containing "bb" and "ccc".
filter() has not actually processed any elements yet -- it has only recorded a step in the pipeline; nothing runs until a terminal operation is invoked.
This code throws an exception immediately, because a Stream cannot be assigned to a variable without a terminal operation.
filter() eagerly evaluates and discards "a" right away, but leaves "bb" and "ccc" unprocessed until a terminal operation runs.
assessments.explanation: Option B correctly describes stream laziness: intermediate operations like filter build up a pipeline description without processing any elements at the moment they're called -- nothing actually runs until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, count, and so on) is eventually invoked on the pipeline. Option A is wrong because it assumes eager evaluation, which streams specifically do not do. Option C is wrong -- assigning an intermediate Stream to a variable with no terminal operation yet attached is completely legal and compiles/runs without any exception; it simply hasn't done anything yet. Option D is a plausible-sounding but incorrect middle ground -- filter() does not partially evaluate anything; either the whole pipeline runs, when a terminal operation demands it, or none of it does.

assessments.prompt: Someone on your team says streams are 'just a fancy way to write a for-loop' and doesn't see why laziness or the single-use rule matter in practice. Explain why they actually do matter, with a concrete scenario for each.
assessments.modelAnswer: Streams differ from a for-loop in two ways that have real, observable consequences, not just stylistic ones. First, laziness: none of a stream's intermediate operations -- filter, map, sorted, and so on -- actually process any elements when they're called; they only build up a description of a pipeline. Nothing runs until a terminal operation, like collect or forEach, is invoked, at which point elements are pulled through the whole chain. This matters concretely in two ways: it enables genuine short-circuiting, so an operation like findFirst() or anyMatch() can stop pulling elements through the pipeline the moment it has its answer, without ever touching the rest of a large (or even conceptually infinite) source -- something a naive for-loop written by hand would need to replicate manually with an explicit break. It also means that if you build a pipeline and forget to attach a terminal operation at all, the whole thing silently does nothing at run time, which is a genuinely different failure mode from a for-loop, where forgetting to 'finish' the loop isn't really a coherent mistake to make in the same way -- it's worth knowing this so an accidentally terminal-operation-less pipeline doesn't get mistaken for a bug somewhere else. Second, the single-use rule: a Stream can be traversed exactly once; once any terminal operation has run on it, that stream is consumed, and calling anything else on that same reference throws IllegalStateException. This is a real trap in practice when someone tries to reuse one stream variable for two different purposes -- say, counting how many elements match a condition, and then separately collecting the transformed matches into a list -- because it's easy to assume a stream behaves like a List you can iterate as many times as you want. The fix is simply to build a fresh stream, from the same source, for each pipeline you need to run, which is cheap and exactly what streams are designed for, but it does require internalizing that a Stream reference is a one-shot pipeline, not a reusable collection.

assessments.prompt: Stream<String> s = List.of("a", "b").stream(); long count = s.count(); List<String> upper = s.map(String::toUpperCase).collect(Collectors.toList()); What happens on the second statement operating on s?
options: It works fine, producing [A, B], since count() only reads from the stream without actually consuming it.

It throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed, because count() is itself a terminal operation, and once any terminal operation has run on a stream, that same stream reference is fully consumed and can never be operated on again.
It silently returns an empty list, since the stream's elements were already used up by count() and none remain to map.
It recomputes the stream from scratch internally, since Stream objects automatically refresh themselves each time a new operation is chained onto them.
assessments.explanation: count() is a terminal operation, even though it superficially looks like a harmless read -- and the moment any terminal operation runs, the stream it ran on is considered consumed. Calling .map(...) on that same, already-consumed s reference afterward throws IllegalStateException at run time. Option A is wrong because there is no such thing as a 'read-only,' non-consuming terminal operation in the Stream API -- every terminal operation consumes the stream it's called on. Option C invents a silent-failure behavior Java's streams don't have; the actual failure is a loud, immediate exception. Option D describes a self-refreshing behavior streams simply don't implement -- a Stream is a genuinely one-shot pipeline over its source, not a renewable view.

assessments.prompt: Optional<Integer> result = Stream.<Integer>empty().reduce((a, b) -> a + b); What does this evaluate to, and why does this form of reduce return an Optional at all rather than an int directly?
options: It returns Optional.empty(), because the one-argument reduce overload has no identity value to fall back on for an empty stream, so it has to express 'no result' explicitly rather than inventing an arbitrary answer.
It throws NoSuchElementException immediately, because reduce always requires at least one element to combine, empty stream or not.
It returns Optional.of(0), because 0 is used as an implicit default identity value whenever none is explicitly supplied to reduce.
It fails to compile, because reduce can only ever be called with exactly two arguments: an identity value and a combining function.
assessments.explanation: The single-argument reduce(BinaryOperator<T>) overload has no identity value supplied by the caller, so for a genuinely empty stream there's no combining to do and no starting value to fall back on and hand back as-is -- there is, correctly, no sensible T to return. Rather than picking an arbitrary placeholder, this overload returns Optional<T>, forcing the caller to explicitly handle the empty case, and for an empty stream that Optional is empty. Option B is wrong -- reduce does not throw for an empty stream when using this overload; that's exactly the scenario Optional is there to represent safely. Option C invents a default identity that doesn't exist for this overload; 0 is never assumed. Option D is wrong because reduce has multiple legitimate overloads, including this exact one-argument form used here.

assessments.prompt: Which statement accurately distinguishes filter and map from sorted and distinct, in terms of stateless versus stateful stream operations?
options: filter and map are stateful because they can reject or transform elements, while sorted and distinct are stateless because they merely reorder or deduplicate what's already there.

filter and map are stateless -- deciding what to do with one element only ever requires that element's own value, never any knowledge of other elements; sorted and distinct are stateful -- sorted cannot know an element's correct final position until every other element has been seen, and distinct must remember every element it's already emitted.
There is no real distinction between the four operations; all are implemented identically internally and differ only in which lambda is supplied to them.
filter and map are stateful because they each require a Predicate or Function argument, while sorted and distinct take no arguments at all and are therefore stateless.
assessments.explanation: filter and map process each element independently, using only that element's own value -- nothing about handling one element depends on having seen any other. sorted, by contrast, cannot place any element into its final position without having compared it against every other element in the stream, and distinct has to remember every distinct value already emitted so far to recognize a later repeat -- both genuinely depend on more than just the one element currently being processed, which is what makes them stateful. Option A gets the labels backwards. Option C is wrong because the stateless/stateful distinction is a real, documented property with real consequences for buffering and parallel behavior, not a cosmetic difference. Option D bases the distinction on argument count, which isn't the actual criterion at all -- sorted() can even take a Comparator argument and remains just as stateful.

concepts.title: Optional and Records: Modern Alternatives to Null Checks and Boilerplate
concepts.description: Optional<T> makes 'this might not have a value' part of a method's return type instead of a silent possibility every caller has to remember on their own, and records give a one-line, immutable alternative to the hand-written getters, constructor, equals, hashCode, and toString every plain data class used to need.
learningObjectives: Explain what problem Optional<T> is designed to solve as a return type, compared to returning null.
Use isPresent/isEmpty, map, orElse, orElseGet, and orElseThrow correctly, and explain why calling get() unconditionally is discouraged.
Explain why Optional is intended primarily as a return type, not as a field type or a method parameter type.
Declare a record and explain precisely what the compiler generates for it automatically.
Explain what it means for a record to be implicitly final and unable to extend another class, and how a compact constructor can validate its components.

sections.heading: The Problem With null as 'No Result': Optional<T> Makes Absence Explicit
sections.body:
A method like `findUserById(int id)` genuinely might not find anything -- the id might not exist. Returning `null` to represent that is legal and extremely common, but it puts the entire burden of remembering to check for it on every single caller, forever, with zero help from the compiler: `User user = findUserById(id); user.getName();` compiles perfectly fine whether or not `findUserById` actually found anything, and if it didn't, that `.getName()` call throws `NullPointerException` -- often far from wherever the actual missing-user condition first occurred, which is exactly what makes tracking down the root cause of an NPE in a large codebase so often tedious.

`Optional<T>` reframes this: instead of returning a `User` that might secretly be `null`, a method returns an `Optional<User>` -- a small wrapper that explicitly represents 'either a `User` is present, or it is not,' visible directly in the method's signature. This doesn't make it *impossible* to mishandle absence (`Optional` still has a `get()` that can throw), but it does make the possibility of 'no result' part of the type itself, which is a much stronger signal to a caller reading the method's signature than a bare `User` that happens to sometimes be `null` with no indication of that in the type at all.

sections.heading: Using Optional Correctly: map, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow
Where Optional Doesn't Belong: Fields, Parameters, and Collections
sections.body: `Optional` was specifically designed as a **return type** for the 'this operation might not produce a result' case -- not as a general-purpose replacement for `null` everywhere in a program. Using `Optional<String>` as a class field, or as a constructor or method *parameter* type, is widely discouraged, for a fairly blunt reason: an `Optional`-typed field or parameter can *still itself be null* (nothing prevents `Optional<String> name = null;`), so you haven't actually eliminated the null-handling problem there -- you've just added an extra layer of unwrapping ceremony (`Optional` isn't `Serializable` either, which occasionally matters for fields specifically). Similarly, prefer returning an empty `List<T>` over `Optional<List<T>>` when a collection might have nothing in it -- an empty collection already represents 'nothing here' perfectly well, without needing to wrap it in another layer to express the same idea a second time.

sections.heading: Records: Concise, Immutable Data Carriers
sections.body:
A huge fraction of classes in any real Java codebase exist purely to hold a fixed set of values together -- a coordinate, a range, a result pair -- and used to require writing out a constructor, private final fields, accessor methods, and correct `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()` implementations by hand, every single time. A **record** (Java 16+) generates all of that from one line:

```java
record Point(int x, int y) { }
```

This single declaration gives you: private final fields `x` and `y`; a canonical (all-arguments) constructor; public accessor methods named exactly after each component -- `x()` and `y()`, deliberately **not** `getX()`/`getY()`; and `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()` implementations based on all of the record's components. Two `Point` instances constructed with the same `x` and `y` are `.equals()` to each other and produce an identical `toString()` (`Point[x=3, y=4]`), with none of that written by hand.

Records are **implicitly final** (no subclass can extend a record) and implicitly extend `java.lang.Record` (so a record cannot extend any other class) -- though a record is completely free to **implement** interfaces, just like any other class. Once constructed, a record's components can never be reassigned; there are no generated setters of any kind, only the generated accessors.

sections.heading: Compact Constructors and Records' Sharp Edges

examples.title: Optional Instead of null, End to End
examples.explanation: Map.get(id) returns null when the key isn't found, so Optional.ofNullable wraps that possibly-null result into an explicit Optional<String> rather than letting a bare null escape findNameById's return value. From there, .map(...) only runs its lambda if a name is actually present -- for id 99, which doesn't exist in USERS, map is simply skipped and orElse's fallback string is used instead, with no null check written anywhere by the caller. This whole chain -- map then orElse -- reads as a fluent description of 'if present, transform it; otherwise, use this default,' entirely replacing what would otherwise be an explicit if (name != null) { ... } else { ... } check.

examples.title: orElse vs orElseGet: When the Default Is Expensive
examples.explanation: present already holds a value, so both a and b end up as "actual-value" -- but the two calls get there very differently. present.orElse(expensiveDefault()) evaluates expensiveDefault() as a normal Java method argument, BEFORE orElse is even called, regardless of whether present turns out to have a value or not -- so "computing expensive default..." prints even though the result is immediately thrown away. present.orElseGet(EagerVsLazyDefault::expensiveDefault) instead passes a Supplier reference, which orElseGet only actually invokes internally if the Optional turns out to be empty -- since present has a value here, the supplier is never called at all, and "computing expensive default..." never prints a second time. This is exactly why orElseGet, not orElse, is the correct choice whenever computing the fallback value costs real time or resources.

examples.title: A Record vs the Equivalent Hand-Written Class
examples.explanation: The record declaration alone generates private final fields x and y, accessor methods x() and y() (not getX()/getY()), and value-based equals(), hashCode(), and toString() -- all of the boilerplate sketched out in the commented equivalent class below it. The compact constructor, public Point { ... }, adds validation logic without repeating the parameter list a second time; the actual field assignments (this.x = x; this.y = y;) happen automatically right after the compact constructor's own body finishes, so there's no need to write them explicitly. p1.equals(p2) is true even though p1 and p2 are two separate objects, because the generated equals() compares the actual component values (3 and 4 in both), not object identity -- exactly the value-based semantics you'd otherwise have to implement by hand, correctly, including a matching hashCode().

misconceptions.description: Since Optional makes the possibility of absence explicit in the type, calling .get() on an Optional is always a safe way to retrieve its value.
misconceptions.clarification: get() throws NoSuchElementException immediately if the Optional is empty -- wrapping a value in Optional doesn't make retrieving it automatically safe, it just makes the possibility of absence visible in the method's return type. Calling get() unconditionally, without first checking isPresent() (or, better, without ever calling get() at all and instead using orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, or map/ifPresent), reproduces exactly the same 'forgot to handle the missing case' bug that Optional exists to help prevent -- just manifesting as a different exception name than NullPointerException.

misconceptions.description: Records are essentially mutable data classes with less boilerplate -- you just don't have to write get/set methods by hand.
misconceptions.clarification: Records are immutable by construction, not merely boilerplate-reduced. Every component becomes a private final field, and the compiler generates only accessor methods (x(), not getX(), and specifically no setters of any kind). There is no way to change a record instance's state after it's constructed -- if a computation needs a 'changed' version of a record's data, the idiomatic approach is to construct a brand-new record instance with the updated values, exactly the same pattern used for immutable types like String.

exercises.prompt: This method looks up a discount code and applies it, but it crashes with NoSuchElementException whenever the code doesn't exist. Find the bug and fix it so a missing code produces a clear, deliberate error instead.
hints: rate.get() throws NoSuchElementException immediately whenever rate is empty -- when does CODES.get(code) return null, causing that to happen here?
Rather than calling get() unconditionally, use a method on Optional designed specifically for the 'produce a clear error if absent' case.
orElseThrow(() -> new SomeException("message")) lets you throw a deliberate, informative exception instead of relying on Optional's own generic NoSuchElementException.
exercises.solutionExplanation: CODES.get("EXPIRED") returns null because that key isn't in the map, so Optional.ofNullable wraps it into an empty Optional -- and the original code's unconditional rate.get() throws NoSuchElementException the moment that happens, with only a generic message that doesn't say which code was the problem. The fix replaces get() with orElseThrow(() -> new NoSuchElementException("Unknown discount code: " + code)), which still throws when the Optional is empty, but with a deliberate, specific, informative message instead of Optional's own generic one -- and it makes the failure path an explicit design choice rather than an accidental consequence of calling get() without checking. Calling getDiscountRate("SAVE10") still works normally, printing 0.1, since that code IS present in CODES.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? Pay attention to exactly what gets compared, and how, by the record's generated equals() method.
hints: a == b compares object identity, exactly the same == rule that applies to any reference type -- are a and b the same object in memory, or two separate ones?
a.equals(b) uses the record's automatically generated equals(), which compares the actual component VALUES of x and y, not object identity.
Records also generate a toString() that follows a fixed format: ClassName[component1=value1, component2=value2].
exercises.solutionExplanation: a == b is false because a and b are two separate objects created by two separate new Coordinate(...) calls -- == on a reference type always compares object identity, and records don't change that rule at all, only equals() is generated specially. a.equals(b) is true because the record's generated equals() compares the actual component values (x=5, y=10 in both), and they match exactly. a.equals(c) is false because c has y=11, which differs from a's y=10 -- even one differing component makes the generated equals() return false. Finally, a's generated toString() follows records' fixed format, printing the class name followed by each component name and value in declaration order: Coordinate[x=5, y=10].

assessments.prompt: Which of the following is generated automatically by declaring `record Money(String currency, long cents) { }`, with no additional code written?
options: Private final fields for currency and cents, accessor methods currency() and cents(), and value-based equals(), hashCode(), and toString() -- but no setters of any kind, since records are immutable.
Private final fields, getCurrency()/getCents() accessor methods following JavaBean naming, and mutator methods setCurrency()/setCents() for updating the values later.
Only a constructor -- accessor methods, equals(), hashCode(), and toString() must still be written by hand.
A mutable class with public fields currency and cents that can be reassigned directly from outside the class.
assessments.explanation: Option A correctly lists what a record generates: private final fields for each component, accessor methods named exactly after the components (currency(), cents() -- not getCurrency()/getCents()), and equals()/hashCode()/toString() implementations based on all components -- with no setters, because records are immutable by design. Option B is wrong on the accessor naming (records deliberately don't use the getX() JavaBean convention) and wrong that setters are generated at all -- they never are. Option C understates what's generated; records produce far more than just a constructor, that's the entire point of using one. Option D is wrong on every count -- record fields are private, not public, and there is no way to reassign a record's components after construction.

assessments.prompt: Explain why Optional is generally recommended as a return type but discouraged as a field type or parameter type, and separately explain what a record's compact constructor is for and what actually happens to the record's fields after it runs.
assessments.modelAnswer: Optional<T> earns its usefulness specifically as a return type for methods where 'no result' is a legitimate, expected outcome -- it puts that possibility directly into the method's signature, which is a much stronger, more visible signal to a caller than a bare T that might secretly be null with no indication of that in the type at all. That value doesn't carry over cleanly to fields or parameters, though, for a fairly concrete reason: an Optional-typed field or parameter can still itself be null -- nothing about declaring a field as Optional<String> prevents someone from assigning it null directly -- so you haven't actually removed the null-handling problem in that context, you've only added an extra unwrapping step (calling .get() or .orElse(...)) on top of a problem that's still there underneath. Optional also isn't designed to be a general-purpose null-replacement -- it's specifically meant for the 'method might not produce a result' shape, which return types have and fields/parameters generally don't need in the same way; a field either has a value because the object was constructed with one, or the class's own design should make clear what 'no value' means for that field without introducing another wrapper type to express it. As for records: a compact constructor is written without repeating the record's parameter list, and it exists specifically to add validation or normalization logic to the values being used to construct the record. Critically, it does NOT replace the actual field assignments -- those still happen automatically, but only AFTER the compact constructor's own body finishes running. So a compact constructor's job is purely to check or transform the incoming values (throwing an exception on invalid input, for instance) before the implicit assignment step takes over and actually sets each private final field to its corresponding parameter's value.

assessments.prompt: Optional<String> present = Optional.of("value"); String result = present.orElse(computeExpensiveDefault()); -- assuming computeExpensiveDefault() has an observable side effect, like printing a message, what happens when this line runs, even though present already holds a value?
options: computeExpensiveDefault() is never called at all, since present already has a value and the default is unnecessary.

computeExpensiveDefault() is called and its side effect runs, because orElse's argument is evaluated eagerly as an ordinary method argument before orElse itself is even invoked -- regardless of whether the Optional turns out to be present or empty.
computeExpensiveDefault() is called, but its side effects are automatically suppressed until Java confirms the Optional is actually empty.
This throws an exception, because orElse cannot legally be called on an Optional that already has a value present.
assessments.explanation: Method arguments in Java are evaluated before the method they're passed to is invoked, with no special exception for orElse -- so computeExpensiveDefault() runs, side effects and all, as an ordinary part of evaluating this statement, whether or not present later turns out to have a value. Since present does have a value here, the computed default is simply discarded once orElse decides it isn't needed -- but by then the work (and the side effect) has already happened. Option A describes orElseGet's actual laziness, not orElse's. Option C invents a suppression mechanism Java doesn't have -- side effects, once triggered by running code, cannot be selectively undone. Option D is wrong -- orElse is always legal to call regardless of whether the Optional is present or empty; that's the entire point of it being a fallback mechanism.

assessments.prompt: record Buffer(byte[] data) { } Buffer b1 = new Buffer(new byte[]{1, 2, 3}); Buffer b2 = new Buffer(new byte[]{1, 2, 3}); System.out.println(b1.equals(b2)); What prints, and why?
options: true, because records always generate value-based equals() that compares every component by its actual content, arrays included.

false, because the generated equals() calls Object.equals() on each component, and arrays never override that method from Object -- so an array component is compared by reference identity rather than content, even though b1's and b2's arrays happen to hold identical bytes.
This fails to compile, because array types are not permitted as record components.
true, because byte[] specifically is treated as a value type inside records, unlike in ordinary hand-written classes.
assessments.explanation: A record's generated equals() compares components using Object.equals() (and generated hashCode() uses Object.hashCode()) for each one -- and arrays never override equals() or hashCode() from Object, so an array component is compared by reference identity, exactly as if you'd compared two plain arrays with == outside of any record at all. b1.data and b2.data are two separate array objects, so even though their contents are identical, b1.equals(b2) is false. Option A overstates records' guarantee -- it holds for ordinary components but specifically breaks down for array-typed ones. Option C is wrong -- arrays are completely legal record component types; they just don't get the value-equality behavior other component types do. Option D is wrong -- there is no special-casing of byte[] or any other array type inside record-generated code; the pitfall applies uniformly to every array-typed component.
